back: Preparing and planting your beds

Compressed (compacted) soil loses its air spaces. Roots slow down. Water enters in a different way. The bed becomes hard to work all year round.

Protecting is easy. Permanent paths, and a bed narrow enough that you reach the middle from both sides.

A width of 1 to 1.2 metres. That is a working number. At that width you can reach the middle from one of the paths, and your feet do not touch the growing area.

Now think about your beds. Can you reach the middle without going inside? Go and try that before you plant anything else.

There is no single bed shape that is right everywhere.

Start with the method that disturbs the soil little [first/most] that solves your problem.

The no-dig method suits most garden soils. Do not disturb its structure; build soil richness on top.

Do not dig wet clay. If soil compaction or poor drainage is very bad, identify the cause by getting local advice before choosing to dig deeper.

Raised beds suit wet ground, where water needs a place to go.

Sunken beds suit dry ground, where you want to catch and keep the rain you get.

Look after heavy rain. Where does water sit or run? Combine what you saw with soil and drainage advice before choosing a bed.

Some plants do not like their roots being disturbed. They grow well when sown directly where they will grow. Beans, carrots and maize are in this group.

Others grow well when they start protected in a seed-raising place (nursery), then are moved to another place. Tomato and brassicas (cabbage-family plants) are in this group.

Use a spacing guide by crop, its variety and local conditions. Check the seed packet and local farmers' advice. Watch for crowding as plants grow.

Before you plant, mark the bed.

Width 1.2 metres. Length three metres. One bed for practice.

Use pegs and string. Mark a rectangle, and mark both access paths.

Then prepare your soil — start with not-digging, and dig deep only when your soil really needs it.

The string line turns an idea into a decision. When the paths exist, keep them. When the growing area exists, protect it.

That bed will be easy to improve all year round, because you stopped walking on it.

back: One bed over three seasons: a fast crop is harvested, then a new sowing goes in beside a slow crop still growing, so the bed is never empty.
Succession planting and intercropping

Succession planting is a calendar habit, not a special crop.

Choose something your household eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, repeatedly.

Plant a short row every two to three weeks.

Spoilage is small when there is an overflowing harvest. Fresh food for a long time. And the work is spread through the season instead of falling on you at once.

Sowing at different times can reduce the risk of losing everything at once. It does not guarantee a harvest if hard conditions continue.

Which fast crop can you sow in small batches? Choose one, start this week.

Here is how it looks in practice.

Sow one alone. Then after two to three weeks, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

In the right season for the crop, harvests can begin to overlap. The first batch is not always ready by the time of the fourth sowing.

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a rule. A cool-season leaf crop can last a long time. Heat can speed things up, or cause the crop to fail.

Watch what your garden does, and adjust the time between sowings. That observation is the real skill.

Intercropping is not just crowding different crops together. Each crop needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The Three Sisters is an example from the farming traditions of Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and they store protein.

Pumpkin spreads on the ground, shades the soil and keeps moisture.

Timing matters. Start the maize first, so it is strong enough to carry the beans when they start climbing.

Crops can compete. Give them suitable space, water and light. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they feed the maize immediately; nutrients in the residue are released during decomposition.

A household can have a hungry gap: weeks when stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.

Yours may come after the stored maize is finished. It may come before the winter greens are ready. It may come in the dry time when water limits the garden.

Do not copy someone else's calendar. Start by naming your months.

Write them down. Then choose a crop and a sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That is planning backwards, and it is what separates a garden that looks productive from a household that really eats.

Staple crops: maize, beans and root vegetables

A staple crop deserves its position because it feeds the household beyond harvest day.

It carries energy or protein. It is stored, or stays in the ground until we need it. And often it carries cultural memory too.

A single staple crop leaves you unprotected. Two or more give you options when weather or pests strike.

Grow at least two. Not one.

Which staple does your household depend on most now? That is the one that would hurt most if it failed — so that is the one that needs a friend.

Each staple protects you from something different.

Maize gives calories, and it stores dry. Open-pollinated (sown naturally) maize allows you even to save your own seed, if you manage isolation and selection.

Beans and cowpeas give a storable protein harvest.

Sweet potato develops some drought tolerance after storage roots have formed. It needs water in the first weeks and while roots are forming; water stress at that time can reduce the harvest. Its young leaves are also edible.

Amadumbe survive in wetter ground, where other staples struggle.

Notice that they fail in different conditions. That is exactly the point.

Resilience does not mean nothing fails.

It means one failure does not end your household's food plan.

One crop is one point of failure.

Two or more staple crops give you more ways to keep eating.

Different crops use water, soil and seasons differently. That difference is protection.

back: Watch and then control pests and diseases

Pest pressure rises for a reason.

Stressed plants. A single crop dominating the ground. Or heavy use of chemicals has already removed predator animals that were helping you.

So before you treat anything, look at the whole system.

Is the plant short of water? Is the soil compacted, or lacking enough nutrients? Are predators already working to solve the problem?

A yellow leaf is not automatically an insect. It can be water, feeding, or root damage. Know which it is before you do anything.

Follow four steps, in order.

First. Look. Look at how the damage appears, the underside of the leaf, the stem, and nearby plants.

Second. Look for stress. Soil moisture, roots, plant spacing, feeding, drainage.

Third. Protect your helpers. Helpful insects do work you would have done.

Fourth. Only after that, do something — and start with the simple thing that works. Physical removal, barriers or a change in plant care can help. Make sure the action fits the problem and watch the results.

If treatment is needed, use a product registered [for] the crop and the pest, and follow its label. This includes neem products. Check safety instructions and the waiting period before harvest. Do not invent mixtures or stronger doses.

Be honest with yourself about which step you always skip.

Harvesting water
Swales, berms, dams, rainwater tanks and greywater — make water move slowly, spread and soak into the ground, every drop.

A concept illustration of a section of a level swale following the contour line, with a raised earth ridge below it. Arrows show runoff water slowing down and spreading; soaking in depends on the soil and the site.
Swales and berms: slowing water on a slope

One kind of swale is a level channel that follows the contour line. It slows runoff and spreads it, so that some water soaks into suitable soil. Some swales are designed with a small controlled slope so they carry excess water gently to a safe place where it exits. Which method suits your land depends on the soil, slope, drainage and storm-water flow. Ask a trained local adviser to check the line, the overflow path and where the water ends up before you dig.

Soil taken out in digging makes a berm (earth ridge) on the downhill side, where trees can be planted when the site design is suitable.

Trees planted there may use moisture stored in the soil after rain, depending on the site.

Heavy rain may fill the swale faster than water soaks into the ground. Plan a safe overflow path before you dig.

The water path must not damage the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. The swale or dam below must be able to receive it safely.

Ask a trained local adviser to check the soil, the slope and storm-water flow. The picture is not a construction design.

The slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable or not. Soil, drainage, unstable ground and water from higher up the mountain all matter.

Keep the soil well covered. Get a local assessment before digging on very 'jumping' [steep], wet or unstable ground. Grass barriers and terraces also need a design that fits the site.

Farm dams and ponds: storing water for the dry season

A dam or pond can store runoff, but the amount available depends on local rainfall, the catchment area, water losses and how much water you use.

Rain seasons vary across South Africa. Use local records and plan for dry periods; there is no promise that the dam will stay full.

Before changing a watercourse or building water-storage works, check the permit needed from the water authority.

A dam needs a site investigation and design by a person properly trained for that. Runoff in the catchment, soil, foundations, downstream risk and a safe spillway all matter.

Do not think annual rainfall tells you the size of a flood or the water you will have stored.

Uncontrolled overflow can erode and break the wall. Plan a safe path for excess water before building.

Water can be lost by evaporation and by seepage into the ground. Check the water level and look for seepage or erosion.

Keep the spillway unblocked and keep the bank cover as specified in the design. Do not plant trees on the wall of an earth dam.

Animals can damage the banks and add dung to the water. Their presence does not make the water clean or safe.

back: Rainwater tanks and roof harvesting: collecting and protecting water

Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on roof size, rainfall and losses.

Check whether the roof materials are suitable for collecting rainwater before connecting a tank.

Use the roof size as seen from above together with local rainfall records. Then estimate water that 'does not succeed' into the gutter, is diverted, or overflows from a full tank.

The annual rainfall figure does not tell you how much water there will be in the dry season. Compare the water you have with the planned use.

Water from the roof can carry dust, droppings and other dirt. A first-flush diverter (a device that diverts the first water) keeps part of the first water out of the tank.

The amount of water to be diverted depends on the roof and the system. Use the supplier's instructions for sizing and maintenance; there is no single volume that suits all roofs.

The diverter does not make the water fit for drinking.

Tank size depends on water demand, rainfall, roof size and the length of dry periods.

Write down the use you plan and estimate your demand using your records. Compare that with the water you have across the seasons.

Plan what you will do when stored water runs low. The province name by itself cannot tell you the tank size you need.

Keep the tank covered, cover openings with a screen to stop insects, and maintain the roof, gutter and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.

Water that looks clean may have germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and treatment suitable for the requested [intended] use.

A basic filter alone is not a guarantee of drinking water. Water used on food crops also needs a safety test.

Household used water (greywater): check before reusing it

Household used water can contain germs, salt, cleaning products and other substances. Guidelines do not describe each source in the same way. South African guidelines differ about kitchen water and laundry water.

Do not include toilet water, nappy water, water from washing a sick person or from washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water with dangerous chemicals.

Before reusing, ask the municipality and a trained local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household water and sanitation services, the requested [intended] use and the site. If this advice is not available or is unclear, do not reuse the water.

A general picture is not a farm design. Soil and mulch do not kill germs in dirty water. Keep it away from drinking-water pipes and prevent contact with people or animals. Do not spray it, let it pond, or let it leave the property to the street, a watercourse or a river.

If a reuse system is already working and the water smells bad, ponds, or harms plants, stop using it and seek hired local advice.
